It defines how the software can be used, modified, and redistributed. This license is what turns regular software into open source, granting developers the right to build on top of others’ work—as long as they comply with specific conditions. Open-source licenses play a vital role in both community-driven and commercial software development. They dictate how companies can integrate open-source components into proprietary products without facing legal or compliance risks. Today, there are over 200 open-source licenses, but in practice, most open-source projects fall under a small number of popular ones. Let’s unpack how these licenses differ and what they mean for your codebase. Learn more about open source. Types of software license: Copyleft and permissive Open-source licenses generally fall into two broad categories: Copyleft licenses A copyleft license requires that any derivative work built from the original open-source code remains open source. Open Source principles go beyond guidelines for clear licensing—they are fundamentally about enabling collaboration. Open Source emphasizes the benefits of collaborative efforts between people who write code, draft documentation, report issues and bugs, implement features, and use the technology. Open Source is about sharing the benefits, as well as the burdens, by promoting the long-term sustainability, quality and maintenance of software projects. Open Source also offers a pathway to make decisions about how projects develop over time, how decisions are made, who and how people contribute, what is prioritized, and what features are added and deprecated. In Open Source projects, project management and governance are affected by the processes, norms, and shared values of participants. Whether it’s a single maintainer, or code-producing nonprofits (e.g., foundations) coordinating thousands of volunteers, the decision-making process affects how Open Source projects evolve. Ultimately, Open Source sets the stage and provides a means for collaboration that benefits those who build the software and those who depend on it, ensuring that changes, improvements, and long-term maintenance are handled in a transparent and predictable way.

passages.text: Open Source software is software distributed under a license that complies with the Open Source Definition (OSD). In plain terms, Open Source software can be used, studied, modified, and shared by anyone without needing further approval from its original authors. Licenses are a legal tool to define and communicate what a user can, can’t, and must do to use a piece of software. To be considered Open Source, software must meet the ten criteria set by the Open Source Initiative’s (OSI) Open Source Definition (OSD). These criteria include allowing free redistribution, providing source code, permitting derivative works, and not discriminating against any use cases (or fields of endeavor), among others. Any license that meets these criteria and is approved by the OSI is considered an “OSI Approved License®.” Well-known examples of licenses that meet the OSD include MIT, Apache 2.0, GPL, and BSD, all of which allow anyone to use, modify, and share the software for any purpose. “Open Source” does not simply mean you have access to the source code. Open source is not to be confused with open standards. Open source refers to software whose source code is freely available for anyone to use, modify and share. An example of this is the Linux operating system, which is developed collaboratively by a global community. In contrast, open standards are publicly available guidelines that ensure interoperability between different technologies. For instance, Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is an open standard that defines how web browsers and servers communicate. While open source software might implement open standards to ensure compatibility, they are distinct concepts. Open source is about making the software code accessible, while open standards focus on setting rules for how different systems work together. Common development and distribution license (CDDL) Created by Sun Microsystems, the CDDL is a weak copyleft license modeled after the MPL. It requires that source code files containing CDDL-licensed code remain open source, but other files in the same project can be under different licenses. You must: - Retain copyright and attribution notices, - Identify yourself as a modifier, and - Include the license in all redistributions. This structure enables collaborative reuse without forcing full project openness. Eclipse public license (EPL) The EPL is another weak copyleft license that applies per file. If you modify EPL code and distribute it, that modified file must stay under EPL. However, your proprietary code can remain closed if kept separate. Definitions and controversies [edit | edit source] Open source software is mainly defined according to The Open Source Definition (OSD) established by the Open Source Initiative (OSI). To qualify as open source under this framework, software must provide its source code and be distributed under a license meeting the ten OSD criteria, notably including non-discrimination against persons, groups, or fields of endeavor – enabling anyone to use, modify, and redistribute it for any purpose. The definition was based on the Debian Free Software Guidelines, written and adapted primarily by Bruce Perens and Eric S. Raymond.[8][9][10] The OSI maintains a list of approved licenses that conform to the OSD.[11] Public-domain software is a source of disagreement as to whether it qualifies as open source software, carrying no formal licence and granting rights that vary significantly depending on the jurisdiction.[12][13] The OSI has stated that public-domain software is "effectively open source, or open source for most practical purposes", when permitted by law, but has declined to certify the public domain as open-source, as the OSI cannot guarantee that public-domain software is OSD-compliant in
